Father is an important title for God. Both God and Father refer to God. This phrase could mean (1) God is both God and Father to our Lord Jesus, or (2) God is Father to our Lord Jesus.
Here, all could refer to: (1) time; (2) quantity.
1:4: Paul uses the word ourselves to emphasize that we, even though we are weak human beings, can comfort others as God comforted us.
1:5: Here Paul speaks of the sufferings of Christ as if they were objects that could increase and move toward him.
Here Paul speaks of comfort as if it were an object that could increase in size.
1:8: Here, Paul is speaking of tribulation as if it were a heavy weight that they had to carry.

Paul is comparing the certainty of death that they experienced to that of someone who receives a sentence of death, that is, an order from a judge that he must be executed.
Here, raising the dead is an idiom for causing someone who has died to become alive again.
1:10: Here, so great a death represents the terrible persecution that Paul and his companions were experiencing and that they were convinced would end in death.
The implication is that God will rescue Paul and his companions from similar dangerous situations in the future.
1:11: Paul is using faces to represent people.

Paul assumes that his readers will understand that the word boasting here is used in the positive sense of wanting to tell others your feelings of great satisfaction and joy in doing something well.
Here, Paul speaks of his conscience as if it were a person who could testify.
The phrase we conducted ourselves means that Paul and his companions controlled their own actions.
Paul is using the world to represent people who live in the world, that is, people in general.
Here, fleshly represents what is natural and human as opposed to what is spiritual and godly.
1:13: This expression could mean: (1) Paul hopes that the Corinthians will understand everything that he is trying to say to them; (2) Paul hopes that the Corinthians will continue to understand what he is saying to them until Jesus returns.
1:14: The implication is that the word boasting here is used in the positive sense of wanting to tell others your feeling of great satisfaction and joy in something good.
1:15: Here, before could mean: (1) Paul intended to visit the Corinthians before going to Macedonia; or (2) Paul intended to visit the Corinthians before he changed his plans.
1:16: Here, you represents the place where the Corinthians live.
ὑφ’ ὑμῶν προπεμφθῆναι εἰς τὴν Ἰουδαίαν
Paul is referring in a polite way to the Corinthians giving him money and food by using the phrase be sent ahead … by you.

Paul is using the question form here to emphasize that he does not make or change his plans according to his own desires.

1:18: Paul is using the term our word to refer to any message that he gave to the Corinthians by using words.

The implication is that God has anointed believers with the Holy Spirit so that they can live for him.
1:22: Paul speaks of God showing that we belong to him as if God had put a visible mark of ownership on us.
Here, Paul is speaking of the Spirit as if the Spirit were a down payment, that is, a partial payment for a purchase with a promise to pay the rest of the amount on a future date.
Here the word hearts refers to the innermost part of a person.
1:23: The phrase I invoke God as a witness upon my soul could be: (1) an oath formula.

1:24: Here, stand firm means to be steady, resolute, or established.
2:1: Here the phrase for myself indicates that Paul made this choice because of reasons he thought about. In other words, he was not forced to make this choice.

Here, the word again implies that Paul has already visited the Corinthians in sorrow. He does not give many details about this visit. It cannot be the first time that he visited the Corinthians, so he must have visited them again in sorrow sometime between when he first met them and when he wrote this letter.
Here the ones who experience the sorrow could be: (1) Paul and the Corinthians; (2) just the Corinthians.
2:2: Paul does not ask this question because he is looking for information. Rather, he asks it to involve the Corinthians in what he is arguing.
2:3: Here Paul refers to a letter he had already written to the Corinthians. Most likely, he wrote this letter sometime between when he wrote 1 Corinthians and 2 Corinthians, but we do not have the letter, so we do not know for sure.
Paul assumes that his readers will understand his meaning. This clause could indicate that it is necessary for: (1) Paul to rejoice in the Corinthians; (2) for the Corinthians to give “joy” to Paul.
ἡ ἐμὴ χαρὰ πάντων ὑμῶν ἐστιν
Paul could be stating that his joy: (1) leads to the Corinthians’ joy; (2) has the same source as the Corinthians’ joy; (3) comes from the Corinthians’ joy.
2:4: Here, the phrase I wrote again refers to the previous letter.
In Paul’s culture, the heart is the place where humans think and feel.
Here, the phrase through many tears indicates what Paul was doing while he wrote the letter. The word tears refers to the act of crying or weeping.

Paul assumes that his readers will understand that the phrase more abundantly could indicate that: (1) Paul has “abundant” love for the Corinthians; (2) Paul loves the Corinthians more than he loves other people.
2:5: Here Paul could be indicating that the person has: (1) grieved Paul some, but mostly the person has grieved the Corinthians; (2) not grieved Paul at all but only the Corinthians.

Here, the phrase in part indicates that only some of an action or group is involved. In this case, Paul could be using in part to refer to: (1) how many of the Corinthians have been grieved; (2) how much the Corinthians have been grieved.

Here, to burden someone refers to placing a heavy object on someone’s back. Paul could be using the phrase I might not burden to refer to: (1) how he is trying to avoid saying too much about the situation. In other words, Paul uses the phrase in part because he does not want to make his words too strong, which would make the words like a person carrying a heavy load; (2) how he wants to avoid troubling or distressing all of them, which would be like “burdening” them with a heavy object.
2:6: Here, the word sufficient could indicate that the punishment: (1) has been severe enough; (2) has lasted long enough.
2:7: μή πως τῇ περισσοτέρᾳ λύπῃ, καταποθῇ ὁ τοιοῦτος
Here Paul speaks as if a person could be overwhelmed or swallowed up by sorrow. He speaks in this way to indicate that a person can experience so much sorrow that it controls and destroys them.
2:9: Here, the phrase I also wrote again refers to the letter that Paul sent to them before he wrote 2 Corinthians.
Here, the phrases for this reason and so that both introduce the purpose for which Paul wrote the previous letter. Paul uses this repetition to emphasize his purpose.

Here, the word proof refers primarily to the results of a test or trial. In this case, Paul is saying that he wants to know how they did on the test, which were the commands he included in the previous letter.
Here, Paul does not state to whom they are obedient. He could be implying that they are obedient to: (1) him as an apostle; (2) God and God’s commands.
2:10: Here Paul could be making: (1) a specific statement about forgiving the person who “grieved” the Corinthians; (2) a general concluding statement about forgiveness.

This clarification fits with what Paul said in 2:5 about how the person did not “grieve” him but rather the Corinthians. Paul could be saying that: (1) he does not have very much to forgive, since the person only hurt him a little; (2) he really has nothing to forgive, since the person hurt the Corinthians, not him.
The phrase for your sake could mean that: (1) Paul forgives the person in order to benefit or help the Corinthians; (2) Paul forgives the person because the Corinthians forgave him.

Here, the phrase in the presence of Christ could indicate that: (1) Paul forgives because he knows that Christ sees or knows what he does. So, he acts in a way that pleases Christ; (2) Paul forgives with Christ as witness; (3) Paul forgives as someone who represents Christ.
2:11: Here the author uses a figure of speech that expresses a strong positive meaning by using a negative word together with a word that is the opposite of the intended meaning.
2:12: Here Paul speaks of God providing opportunities for him to preach the gospel as if God were “opening” a door for the gospel. The image is of God opening a door so that Paul can go in and preach the message about Christ.

Here Paul uses the spatial metaphor in the Lord to describe his union with Christ. In this case, being in the Lord, or united to the Lord, shows that the door was opened to Paul: (1) by the Lord; (2) so that he could continue to serve in his union with the Lord.
Here, the word Lord could refer to: (1) Jesus the Messiah; (2) God generally.

οὐκ ἔσχηκα ἄνεσιν τῷ πνεύματί μου

Here Paul does not clarify what he was concerned or anxious about. He clarifies later in 7:5–16 that he was anxious to know how Titus’ visit to the Corinthians went. The Corinthians would have made this inference, since Titus had already visited them.
τῷ μὴ εὑρεῖν με Τίτον τὸν ἀδελφόν μου
Here Paul is stating that Titus was not in Troas, not that he simply could not find him.

Here Paul speaks of Titus as if he were his brother (probably a younger brother). He speaks in this way to indicate that Titus is a fellow believer and that he and Paul are as close as if they were brothers.
Here Paul refers to how he said farewell to the people from Troas, but he also means that he left their city.
2:14: Here Paul speaks as if God were a leader who had won a victory and set up a parade or triumphal procession to celebrate. In this parade, Paul and his fellow workers could be either or both of the following: (1) prisoners who have been conquered and who are put in the parade to illustrate the victory. This is the normal meaning of the word in other places; (2) soldiers who helped win the victory and who are celebrating. This is not the normal meaning of the word, but it is possible and fits the context well.

Paul uses the spatial metaphor in Christ to describe the union of believers with Christ. In this case, being in Christ, or united to Christ, explains why or how they are involved in the triumphal procession.

Here Paul speaks as if the knowledge of him were an aroma, a smell or odor. In this case, the context implies that this is a pleasing or good smell. He speaks in this way to indicate that everyone hears and reacts to the message about Christ, just like everyone smells and reacts to a strong odor. Also, just like a smell fills a whole room, so the good news fills every place on earth.

Here Paul speaks as if God used him and his fellow workers to make God known in every place. The Corinthians would have understood him to mean that God uses them to make God known in many places, or in every place that they visit.
2:15: Here Paul continues to speak about fragrance and good smells (See: 2:14). He identifies himself and his fellow workers as a fragrance that comes from Christ and which goes toward God. By speaking in this way, he shows that we are those who represent or declare who Christ is in the presence of God. Just like everyone smells a good smell and knows where it comes from, so everyone notices Paul and his fellow workers and realizes that they represent Christ before God.
2:16: Here Paul continues to speak about fragrance and good smells (See: 2:14–15). He specifically explains what kind of aroma he and his fellow workers are. Those who do not believe think that the aroma smells bad, while those who do believe think that the aroma smells good.

Twice here Paul uses the words from and to with the same word. He could be using this form because: (1) from indicates the source of the aroma, and to indicates the effects of the aroma; (2) from and to together emphasize that the aroma is characterized completely by either death or life.

Paul does not ask this question because he is looking for information. Rather, he asks it to involve the Corinthians in what he is arguing. The question could imply that the answer is that: (1) Paul and his fellow workers are sufficient since God works through them; (2) no one is sufficient.
2:17: Here, the word peddling refers to the practice of selling goods that one has. The word implies that the person who is peddling is trying to make as much profit as they can, whether by honest or deceitful means.
Here, the word word represents what someone says in words.
Here, the phrase as from God indicates that God sent Paul and his fellow workers to speak the gospel. The word as indicates how they speak. It does not mean that they are not really from God.
Here, Paul implies that they are speaking the word of God that he already mentioned.

Here, the phrase in the presence of God could indicate that: (1) they speak as they do because they know that God sees or knows what they do. So, they speak in a way that pleases God; (2) they speak with God as a witness guaranteeing what they say.
Paul uses the spatial metaphor in Christ to describe the union of believers with Christ. In this case, being in Christ, or united to Christ, explains how they speak.
3:1: Paul does not ask this question because he is looking for information. Rather, he asks it to involve the Corinthians in what he is arguing.
Here, the word again implies that Paul and his fellow workers had already “commended themselves” at some point in the past. Most likely, this happened when they first met the Corinthians.
Paul does not ask this question because he is looking for information. Rather, he asks it to involve the Corinthians in what he is arguing.
3:2: Here Paul continues to speak about “letters,” but now he tells the Corinthians that they themselves are the letter of recommendation for Paul and his fellow workers. This letter is not a physical document, but is written in their hearts, and all men can read it. Paul speaks in this way to indicate that the recommendation he relies on is the Corinthian believers. In other words, the fact that they believe and that they are close with Paul (in our hearts) shows that Paul is trustworthy and a true apostle.
Here the word translated as yourselves emphasizes You.

In the Paul’s culture, hearts are the places where humans think and plan. What Paul means is that the recommendation from the Corinthians is not written down on paper but, rather, is a part of their relationship with Paul.
Here, the words known and read express very similar ideas. It is likely that known indicates that people are aware that there is a letter, while read indicates that they know what the letter says.
3:3: Here, the phrase making known could: (1) indicate that something is well-known or obvious to people; (2) state that the Corinthians show or reveal something to others.

Here Paul continues to speak as if the Corinthians were a letter. Here, he states that this letter was written by Christ and administered by Paul and his fellow workers. He means that Christ is the one who enabled the Corinthians to believe, and Christ worked through Paul and his fellow workers to do that. Paul then contrasts a letter written with ink and on tablets of stone with a letter written by the power of the Spirit and on hearts of flesh. What he means by this is that the letter is the Corinthians, not some written document, and that the message is communicated by the Spirit, not by letters written with ink.
Here, the phrase having been administered by us could indicate that: (1) “we” delivered the letter; (2) “we” helped Christ compose the letter.
Here, the word ink refers to colored liquid that people in Paul’s culture used to write letters and words.

Here, the phrase living God identifies God as the one who “lives” and possibly as the one who gives life. The primary point is that God actually lives, unlike inanimate idols and other things that people may call gods.

Here, the word tablets refers to thin, flat pieces of stone on which people would write words, especially important words. Paul may be referring here to the tablets on which Moses wrote God’s commandments (See: Exodus 34:1–4), so, if possible, use a word that could refer to those tablets.
In the Paul’s culture, hearts are the places where humans think and plan. Here Paul states that these hearts are made of flesh, meaning that they are live, functional body parts.
3:4: Here, the phrase toward God could indicate that the confidence is: (1) before or in the presence of God. In other words, Paul has confidence that God approves of him and his fellow workers; (2) in God. In other words, Paul has confidence that God will do what he has promised.
3:5: ἀφ’ ἑαυτῶν ἱκανοί … ἡ ἱκανότης ἡμῶν
Here Paul does not state what they are not sufficient to do. He implies that it is serving God by preaching the gospel.
Here, the word anything refers to whatever they do to serve God well.
3:6: When Paul contrasts letter and Spirit, he implies that letter describes the old covenant and Spirit describes the new covenant. What he means is that the old covenant was only written down and could not change people on the inside. On the other hand, the new covenant is empowered by the Holy Spirit, who can change people on the inside.

Here, the word letter refers generally to a message written using sound-symbols called letters. More specifically, Paul uses the word letter to refer to the old covenant, a written document. It could not change people like the Spirit can.
Here, the word Spirit could refer to: (1) the Holy Spirit; (2) the spirit of a person, or their mind or heart.

Here Paul speaks as if the letter were a person who kills others. He speaks in this way to indicate that the letter (which refers to the old covenant and its regulations) does not have the power to give life but instead can only condemn people to die.
3:7: Here, the word ministry could refer primarily to: (1) the action of ministering. In this case, the word refers to how Moses administered the old covenant; (2) the system of ministry. In this case, the word refers to the old covenant or its laws.

Here Paul refers to how God engraved or carved the regulations for the ministry on stones or tablets. Much as in the previous verse, letters refers to written characters, so the point is that God used writing. Paul is probably referring to the story about how Moses met God on a mountain, and God carved the regulations of the covenant on two pieces of stone.

Here Paul refers to a story about what happened after God engraved the stone tablets. When Moses returned to talk to the Israelites, his face shone brightly because he had been talking to God. In other words, some of God’s glory became part of Moses’ face, and the Israelites could not look intently at his face because it was a little like looking at God.

Here, the word ministry could refer primarily to: (1) the action of ministering. In this case, the word refers to how Paul and his fellow workers administered the new covenant; (2) the system of ministry. In this case, the word refers to the new covenant or its principles.
Here, the word Spirit could refer to: (1) the Holy Spirit; (2) the “spirit” of a person, or their mind or heart.
3:9: Here, the word ministry could refer primarily to: (1) the action of ministering. In this case, the word refers to how people administered the two covenants; (2) the system of ministry. In this case, the word refers to a covenant or its principles.
3:10: Here, the phrase {what} had been glorified refers to the old covenant that God gave through Moses. The phrase surpassing glory refers to the new covenant that Paul and his fellow workers serve.
Here, the phrase in this part indicates that a statement is only true in part or in some specific way.
Here, the phrase in this part and the word because both introduce how or why {what} had been glorified is not glorified. Paul uses both elements because he wants to make his point very clear.
3:11: Here, the phrase fading away translates the same word that Paul used in 3:7 to refer to how the glory was “fading” from Moses’ face. Paul means that just like the glory on Moses’ face was temporary, so the old covenant that God made through Moses was also temporary.
Here, the phrase {what} is fading away refers to the old covenant, while the phrase {what} remains refers to the new covenant.
3:12: Here Paul does not say exactly what it is that we do. He implies that it is the “ministry” that he has referred to in 3:7–11.
3:13: Here Paul contrasts the boldness that he and his fellow workers show with how Moses could not show God’s glory openly. In other words, Paul and his fellow workers can reveal God’s glory openly, in contrast to Moses, who could not.
Here Paul refers to a story in Exodus 34:29–35 that describes how Moses’ face shone with God’s glory after Moses spoke with him. Moses would hide his face with a veil when his face shone like this.
Here the author uses the word sons to refer in general to all the descendants of Israel.

Here, the word end could refer to: (1) the result of the fading, which was that the “glory” completely stopped shining from Moses’ face; (2) the purpose or implication of how the “glory” ceased shining from Moses’ face, which was that the old covenant too would cease.

Here, the phrase {what} was fading away could refer to: (1) the “glory” that shone from the face of Moses. In this case, Paul could also be implying that the old covenant would also “fade.”; (2) the old covenant, that would “fade away” when God instituted a new covenant.
3:14: Here Paul speaks as if people’s minds were a soft substance that could be hardened, becoming resistant to change. He speaks in this way to indicate that their minds could not know or understand what was happening, unlike a soft substance that would change when something impacts it.

Here Paul speaks as if a veil kept people from understanding the old covenant when it is “read,” and this veil is not lifted. He speaks in this way to identify the inability of people to understand the old covenant with how Moses’ kept the Israelites from looking at his face with a veil. Just as the veil kept them from seeing the glory on his face, so a veil keeps people from understanding the reading of the old covenant.
Here, the phrase same veil could refer to: (1) the veil that Moses wore (See: 3:13); (2) the veil that hardened their minds.
Here, the phrase old covenant refers to the words that contain or describe the old covenant.
Here Paul uses the spatial metaphor in Christ to describe the union of believers with Christ.

Here, the phrase fading away is the same phrase that Paul used to describe how the “glory” was “fading” from Moses’ face (See: 3:13). What Paul means is that the veil disappears or is removed in Christ.
3:15: Here, the word Moses could refer to: (1) the first five books of the Old Testament, often called “the Law” or the “Pentateuch.”; (2) the entire Old Testament.
κάλυμμα ἐπὶ τὴν καρδίαν αὐτῶν κεῖται

3:16: Here, the phrase turn to the Lord refers to a how people stop doing whatever they want and instead begin to trust and obey God.
Here, the word Lord could refer to: (1) God generally; (2) Jesus the Messiah.
Here Paul continues to refer to a veil that keeps people from understanding the Scriptures.
3:17: Here, just as in 3:16, the word Lord could refer to God generally or to Jesus specifically.
Here, the word Spirit could refer to: (1) the Holy Spirit; (2) what is “spiritual” as opposed to what is written or fleshly.

The words the Spirit form an important title that describes the Lord. Here Paul could mean that: (1) the “Lord” mentioned in 3:16 is the Holy Spirit; (2) believers encounter God the Lord as the Holy Spirit; (3) the Lord is “spiritual.”

Here Paul speaks of the Spirit being in a place, and so freedom also is in that place. Here he speaks in this way to connect the Spirit and freedom. He means that whoever has the Spirit also has freedom.

Paul is indicating a contrast that could be: (1) with Moses, who had to veil the glory on his face. Unlike him, believers do not need to veil their faces; (2) the Israelites, who could not look directly at the glory of God. Unlike them, believers can see God’s glory directly without a veil.
Here the word translated as reflecting could refer to: (1) acting as a mirror that “reflects” an image; (2) seeing something that is “reflected” in a mirror.
Here, just as in 3:16–17, the word Lord could refer to God generally or to Jesus specifically.
Here, the phrase the same image refers to the image that belongs to the Lord.

Here Paul uses the words from and to with the same word, much as he did in 2:16. He could be using this form because: (1) from indicates the source of the transformation, and to indicates the effects of the transformation; (2) from and to together emphasize that the transformation is characterized completely by glory.
The phrase just as from indicates the source of the transformation.

Here, Paul could be using this phrase to: (1) identify the Lord as the Spirit, as he did in 3:17. Here, the word Spirit could refer to: (1) the Holy Spirit; (2) what is “spiritual” as opposed to what is written or fleshly.

4:2: Here, the phrase shameful hidden things could refer to: (1) things that people “hide” because they are shameful; (2) things that are both hidden and shameful.

Here, the word word represents what someone says in words.

4:4: Here, the phrase the god of this age refers to Satan, or the devil. Paul describes him in this way because God has allowed Satan to have some control or power in this age, which refers to the world as it is right now.
Here Paul speaks as if minds were eyes that could be blinded or that could see light. If minds are blinded, they cannot understand something. If minds can see light, they can understand something.
4:5: Here, the phrase Lord Christ Jesus could: (1) give a title or name for Jesus; (2) state that Christ Jesus is the Lord.
Here Paul could be indicating that he and his fellow workers are servants because of: (1) who Jesus is; (2) what Jesus has done; (3) what Jesus wants Paul and his fellow workers to do.
4:6: Here Paul continues the “light” metaphor from 4:4. When God shined in their hearts, that means that he caused them to understand.
In the Paul’s culture, hearts are considered to be the places where humans think and plan. What Paul means is that God has shined on their thoughts or on what they think.

Here, the glory that is in {face} of Jesus Christ contrasts with the glory that faded on Moses’ face (See: 3:7). What Paul means is that Jesus reveals or shows what God is like, particularly how glorious he is.
4:7: ἔχομεν … τὸν θησαυρὸν τοῦτον ἐν ὀστρακίνοις σκεύεσιν

Here Paul speaks of the knowledge about God’s glory as if it were a treasure, that is, something that is very valuable. He speaks of himself and those who proclaim the gospel as if they were clay jars, which are not valuable and can break easily. He speaks in this way to contrast how valuable and long-lasting the gospel is (the treasure) with how worthless and weak he and those who preach the gospel with him are in comparison (clay jars).
Here, the word jars refers to any type of container that is meant to hold something else. The word clay refers to dirt or mud, which was used to make inexpensive and fragile containers.
4:8: Here, the word every indicates that what Paul is about to describe happens often or in many situations.

Here Paul speaks as if he and his fellow workers were physically being pressed in by other people but not being crushed by them. He speaks in this way to indicate that other people are making his life difficult or trying to hurt him, but they are not fully succeeding.
4:9: Here, Paul speaks as if people physically push him and his fellow workers so that they fall down. By speaking in this way, he is referring to any time people act against or bully him and his fellow workers, which may or may not be physical.
4:10: τὴν νέκρωσιν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἐν τῷ σώματι περιφέροντες

Here Paul speaks as if the dying of Jesus were an object that he and his fellow workers could carry around. He could speak in this way to indicate that: (1) he experiences suffering and pain that are like the dying of Jesus; (2) he and his fellow workers proclaim the dying of Jesus both by what they say and what they do (in the body).

The revelation of the life of Jesus in our body could mean that: (1) the life that Jesus has will become the life that they too have. In other words, like Jesus resurrected, they too will resurrect; (2) they reveal the fact that Jesus is alive. In other words, by carrying around Jesus’ death, they also reveal his resurrection; (3) they are delivered from the sufferings that they experience so that they have life from Jesus.
4:11: Here Paul speaks as if he and his fellow workers were objects that someone could hand over to death. He means that they are under the power of death or are experiencing things related to death, like suffering and hardship.

Here, the phrase for the sake of Jesus could indicate that Paul and his fellow workers are always being handed over to death: (1) to serve Jesus; (2) because of Jesus, particularly because they preach about him.
Here Paul uses words and ideas that are very similar to what he used in the second part of 4:10.
Here, the phrase mortal flesh refers to people who will die.
4:12: Here Paul speaks of death and life as if they were persons who could “work.” He means that he and those will experience things related to death, while the Corinthians experience things related to life.
Here Paul may be: (1) simply contrasting death and life; (2) indicating that the death in them leads to the life in you.
Here, the word life could refer: (1) specifically to resurrection life, which the Corinthians will receive; (2) generally to being alive and not experiencing suffering or dangerous things.
4:13: Here, the word spirit could refer to: (1) a human spirit or attitude, which is characterized by faith; (2) the Holy Spirit, who gives faith.
Here, the word same could indicate that: (1) this is the same spirit that the person who wrote the quotation had; (2) this is the same spirit that the Corinthians also have.
4:14: ὁ ἐγείρας τὸν Ἰησοῦν, καὶ ἡμᾶς … ἐγερεῖ
Paul uses the words raised and raise to refer to someone who had previously died coming back to life.
Here, the phrase with Jesus could indicate that the Paul and his fellow workers will: (1) be where Jesus is; (2) be resurrected as Jesus was; (3) be joined with Jesus.
4:15: Here, the phrase all these things refers to everything that Paul and his fellow workers do and experience as they preach the gospel, including their sufferings (See: 4:7–12) and the message that they preach (See: 4:13–14).
Here Paul implies that the grace comes from God.

Here, the phrase through more and more could indicate that: (1) the grace increases by being received by more people; (2) the grace increases because God uses more situations and experiences to spread the gospel.
4:16: See you how translated the word discouraged in 4:1. It could refer to: (1) losing motivation and confidence; (2) becoming tired or exhausted.
Here, the phrase outer man refers to the part of the person that others can observe and see. It includes the physical part of the person, but it is not only a person’s body.
Here Paul speaks as if the outer man were a dead thing that was decaying. He speaks in this way to indicate that the outer man is in the process of dying or passing away.
Here, the phrase inner {man} could refer to: (1) the part of the person that others cannot observe and see; (2) the spiritual part of the person.
4:17: ἐλαφρὸν τῆς θλίψεως … αἰώνιον βάρος δόξης

Here Paul describes affliction and glory as if they were objects that could be light or have weight. He speaks in this way to indicate how unimportant or insignificant the affliction is compared with how important or significant the glory is.
Here Paul speaks as if the affliction were a process that was producing the glory. He means that the affliction leads to glory for us.
Here, the phrase far beyond all comparison identifies something that is much greater than anything else.
4:18: Here, the word watching refers specifically to focusing on something or paying close attention to something. It does not require the attention or focus to be visual.
5:1: Here Paul speaks as if a person’s body were a house, tent, or building in which that the person lives. This was a common way to refer to a person’s body in Paul’s culture. He identifies the current body as a tent that is torn down, because this body will die. He describes the body that a person will have when God resurrects them as a building from God and an eternal house that is not made with hands. This is an important metaphor in 5:1–9, so preserve the house, tent, and building language if possible.

Many people in Paul’s culture believed that the space that they called “heaven” contained multiple layers or spheres of individual heavens. Here Paul refers to how the eternal house can be found in the heavens. Since Paul does not include details about the heavens, translate heavens with a word or phrase that refers to all of heavenly space, including the idea of multiple heavens if possible.
Here, the word hands refers to the main part of the body that we use to make things. So, the phrase refers to the whole person who makes things.
5:2: Paul also begins to refer to receiving new, resurrection bodies as if they were pieces of clothing that people could put on. This also is an important figure of speech for the following verses, so preserve the language if possible.
5:3: Here Paul continues to speak of bodies as if they were clothing.
Paul could mean that: (1) we clothe ourselves; (2) God clothes us.
5:4: Here Paul continues to speak of bodies as buildings and clothing.

Here Paul speaks as if he and his fellow workers were carrying a heavy burden. He means that something is making their lives difficult. The burden could be: (1) how the tent, that is, their current bodies, falls apart and dies; (2) how other people’s situations make life hard for them.
Here Paul refers to the mortal as if it were food that could be swallowed up. This illustrates that the mortal has been defeated as surely as if life devoured it as food.
5:5: Here, the phrase having prepared could refer to how God: (1) has acted in believers’ lives to get them ready for resurrection and new life; (2) created believers when they first began to live.
Here, Paul is speaking of the Spirit as if he were a down payment, that is, a partial payment for a purchase with a promise to pay the rest of the amount on a future date.
5:6: ἐνδημοῦντες ἐν τῷ σώματι, ἐκδημοῦμεν ἀπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου
Here Paul continues to refer to the body as if it were a building that a person could be at home in.
Paul implies that this body is the one that people have before they die.
5:7: Here, the words faith and sight could refer to: (1) the acts of “believing” or “seeing” Jesus the Messiah; (2) what is “believed” or “seen.”
5:8: Here Paul continues to refer to the body as if it were a building in which a person could be at home.

Here, the word body refers to the body that people have before they die. The phrase be away from the body could refer to: (1) a temporary situation between when a believer dies and when Jesus comes back in which the believer does not have a body but is still with the Lord; (2) the eternal situation of believers, in which they either have no bodies or have new bodies.
5:9: Here Paul could be referring to how people are at home or away from: (1) the Lord; (2) this body.
Here Paul continues to refer to a building in which a person could be at home.
5:10: Here, the phrase judgment seat refers to a raised seat that a judge or official would sit on when he or she was making official decisions. In Paul’s culture, people expected the Messiah to sit on this kind of seat when this world ends and decide whether to reward or punish people. Paul uses this idea to refer to how Jesus will judge us all.

In this context, the phrase receive back refers to getting something in payment or in return for something else. Paul is speaking as if everyone will receive back as payment or recompense exactly what they did through the body. By this, Paul means that God will reward or punish everyone in a way that fits with what they did.
Here, the phrase through the body clarifies that the {things done} are what people did while they had mortal bodies and lived on this earth.
Here, the phrase with regard to what things he did introduces what Christ is judging.
Here, the words good or bad could describe: (1) the things that people did; (2) both the things that people did and what they receive back; (3) just what people receive back.
5:11: Here Paul could be implying that he “persuades” people: (1) to know the fear of the Lord as he and those with him do; (2) to realize that he and those with him are people who know the fear of the Lord and are thus trustworthy; (3) to accept the gospel.
πεφανερώμεθα … ἐν ταῖς συνειδήσεσιν ὑμῶν πεφανερῶσθαι

Here Paul does not state what it is about them that is clearly known. He implies that God knows that Paul and his coworkers are faithful to God and preach the good news properly. Paul wants the Corinthians to recognize this also.
5:12: Here, the word again implies that Paul and those with him had already “commended themselves” at some point in the past. Most likely, this happened when they first met the Corinthians.
In Paul’s culture, the heart is the place where humans think and feel.
5:13: Paul uses two opposite phrases. These phrases could contrast: (1) fanatical or extreme behavior with moderate or sane behavior; (2) ecstatic or visionary behavior with rational or normal behavior.
The phrases for God and for you could indicate: (1) the people for whose benefit Paul is behaving in these ways; (2) the people to whom he directs his behavior.
5:14: Here, the phrase having judged could introduce: (1) what he and those with him think about how the love of Christ controls them; (2) a reason why the love of Christ controls them.
Here, the phrase for the sake of could indicate that Jesus died: (1) to benefit or help others; (2) instead of or in place of others.

Here Paul speaks as if all died because or when Jesus died. Since the following verse states that some people are still “living,” he cannot mean that every person has physically died. He may mean that people have died to sin, or that they participated in how Christ died, or that who they used to be died. Since some or all of these interpretations are possible, preserve the metaphor or express the idea in a form that could allow for several of these interpretations, such as in simile form.
5:15: Here, much as in 5:14, the word for could indicate that Jesus died: (1) to benefit or help others; (2) instead of or in place of others.
Here, the phrase the ones living could identify people who: (1) have spiritual life, that is, those who have received new life in Jesus; (2) have physical life, that is, who have not died.
Here, to live for a person refers to acting in a way that pleases or fulfills that person.
Paul uses the word raised to refer to someone coming back to life after they died.
5:16: Here, the word now could refer to: (1) the time when we believed; (2) the time in which Paul was writing this letter.
Here Paul uses the phrase according to the flesh to refer to human ways of thinking.
5:17: Paul uses the spatial metaphor in Christ to describe the union of believers with Christ. In this case, being in Christ, or united to Christ, indicates that a person believes in Christ and is a Christian.
Here, the phrases old things and new things could refer to: (1) things that characterize a person and their life; (2) the world and how a person experiences it.
Here, the phrase new things could be: (1) the subject of have come; (2) the object of have come, and the subject is the person who is in Christ.
5:18: Here, the phrase all these things could refer to: (1) the “new creation” and “new things” that Paul mentioned in 5:17; (2) everything that exists.
5:19: Here Paul uses the spatial metaphor in Christ to describe the union of believers with Christ.
Here, the word world could refer to: (1) the people in the world; (2) the world as a whole, including people, places, and things.
μὴ λογιζόμενος αὐτοῖς τὰ παραπτώματα αὐτῶν
Here Paul speaks as if God could keep a “count” of people’s trespasses, which means that he would keep track of everything that a person did wrong in order to condemn them.

Here Paul speaks as if the word of reconciliation were an object that God would “place in” Paul and those with him. He means that God has called or commissioned them to proclaim this word of reconciliation.
Here, the word word represents what someone says in words.
5:20: Here, the phrase on behalf of could indicate that: (1) Paul and those with him represent Christ; (2) Paul and those with him act for the benefit of Christ.
Here, the phrase as though introduces the implication or meaning of being ambassadors on behalf of Christ.
Here Paul does not state to whom God is appealing. He could imply that he is appealing to: (1) everyone; (2) the Corinthians specifically.
Here what Paul says could be addressed to: (1) the Corinthians specifically; (2) every person with whom Paul and those with him speak.
5:21: Here, the phrase having known sin refers to committing or doing sin. It does not refer just to knowing about sin.
Here Paul speaks as if God made Jesus sin. He could mean that God: (1) treated Jesus as though he were a sinner; (2) identified Jesus with sinners and sin; (3) caused Jesus to be a sin offering.
Here, the phrase for us could indicate that God made Jesus sin: (1) to benefit or help us; (2) instead of or in place of us.

Here Paul speaks as if people could become the righteousness of God. He could mean that we: (1) share the righteousness that God gives to those who believe; (2) are declared “righteous” by God; (3) become those who live “righteously.”
Here Paul uses the spatial metaphor in him to describe the union of believers with Christ. In this case, being in him, or united to Christ, explains how people become the righteousness of God.
6:1: Here Paul does not directly state with whom he is working. He could be implying that he works with: (1) God, since God is the subject of the previous sentence; (2) the Corinthians, since they are the ones whom is “urging.”

Here, in vain identifies a cause that does not have its intended effect. In this case, receiving the grace of God will not lead to salvation if the Corinthians do not persevere in living as those who have received the grace of God.
6:2: The two clauses in the quotation mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.

Here, the phrase an acceptable time refers to a point in time that someone considers to be a proper or appropriate for doing something. Paul could be implying that this time is acceptable to: (1) God; (2) people.
Here, the word listened indicates that God both listened and responded.

The phrases a day of salvation and a favorable time repeat the words from the quotation exactly, except that Paul uses a word that emphasizes that the time is good (favorable) instead of just being appropriate (acceptable). Use the form that you used in the quotation, although, if possible, use a word for a good time instead of just an acceptable time.
6:3: Here, the phrase giving no cause for offense refers to how a person acts so that others are not offended.
Here, the phrase in anything could refer to: (1) actions and behavior; (2) people.
6:4: ἐν παντὶ συνιστάντες ἑαυτοὺς ὡς Θεοῦ διάκονοι
Here the word as could introduce: (1) who they are (servants of God) while they commend themselves; (2) what it is that they must commend themselves to be.
ἐν θλίψεσιν, ἐν ἀνάγκαις, ἐν στενοχωρίαις

Here, the words tribulations, hardships, and distresses function together to refer to many different kinds of persecution and suffering. It is possible that tribulations refers to direct persecution, hardships refers to being forced to do something difficult, and distresses refers to being unable to do what one wants.
6:6: The phrase in the Holy Spirit could refer to: (1) having the power or help of the Holy Spirit; (2) being “holy” in one’s “spirit.”
6:7: Here, the word word represents what someone says in words.

Here Paul speaks as if righteousness were weapons for the right hand and the left. He means that the righteous way in which he and his fellow workers live their lives is like armor and swords which they use to protect themselves and fight against enemies. Paul does not state who the enemy is, but he implies that it is anyone and anything that acts against God and the gospel.
τῆς δικαιοσύνης τῶν δεξιῶν καὶ ἀριστερῶν

Here, having weapons for the right hand and the left could describe how a soldier: (1) has an offensive weapon in one hand and a defensive weapon in the other; (2) is completely equipped for battle and able to defend against attacks from right and left.
6:8: διὰ δόξης καὶ ἀτιμίας, διὰ δυσφημίας καὶ εὐφημίας
In these two statements, Paul indicates that he and his fellow workers persevere in serving God whether people think and say good things or bad things about them.
Here and in the following two verses Paul uses as to introduce what other people think about him and his fellow workers and then yet to introduce what is really true about them.
6:9: Here and in the following verse Paul uses as to introduce what other people think about him and his fellow workers, and then he uses yet to introduce what is really true about them.
6:10: Here, just as in the previous verse, Paul uses as to introduce what other people think about him and his fellow workers and then yet or but to introduce what is really true about them.

Here Paul speaks as if he and his fellow workers made other people rich. He means that he helps people receive blessings from God, including forgiveness and new life, which makes them spiritually rich.

Here Paul could be stating that they possess: (1) all things that Christ possesses. In other words, because Christ rules over everything, Paul and his fellow workers also possess everything; (2) all spiritual blessings, which are the important things.
6:11: τὸ στόμα ἡμῶν … ἡ καρδία ἡμῶν
Here, the word mouth refers to the action of speaking with the mouth, and the word heart refers to the act of thinking and feeling with the heart.
τὸ στόμα ἡμῶν ἀνέῳγεν πρὸς ὑμᾶς

Here Paul speaks as if he and his fellow workers had opened their mouths toward the Corinthians. He means that he and his fellow workers have spoken what is true, and they have spoken confidently. Paul could be specifically referring to: (1) how he and his fellow workers have interacted with the Corinthians in the past; (2) what he has said in this letter so far; (3) what he said in 6:3–10.
Here Paul speaks as if he and his fellow workers have opened wide their “hearts” to the Corinthians. He means that they love and care for the Corinthians.
6:12: Here Paul speaks about loving others as if it were about having space in one’s insides. When people have space for other people inside them (not restricted), they are loving and caring for others.
6:13: Here, the phrase same exchange refers to how Paul and his fellow workers have “opened their hearts” (that is, shown love) to the Corinthians. This is the first part of the exchange, and now Paul wants the Corinthians to complete this exchange by opening themselves to Paul and his fellow workers.

Here Paul indicates that he is speaking as if he were addressing children. He could mean that: (1) he is using words and ideas that children use, particularly referring to the idea of exchange; (2) he is speaking to the Corinthians as if he was their father and they were his children.
Here Paul continues to speak about loving others as if it were about having space in one’s insides. When people have space for other people inside them, they love and care for them.
6:14: Here Paul refers to a farming practice in which two or more animals were yoked together with a piece of wood that was then connected to a plow or cart. In this way, the animals together pulled the plow or cart. Paul applies this farming practice to people to indicate that believers should not try to accomplish what God wants them to do by working with unbelievers.
Here Paul is using the question form to deny that something could be true.

Here Paul speaks about how light and darkness do not have fellowship. He could be speaking about: (1) things and people that are good (light) and things and people that are evil (darkness); (2) God’s kingdom and people (light) and Satan’s kingdom and people (darkness).
6:15: Here, just as in 6:14, Paul is using the question form to deny that something could be true.
Here, the word Beliar is another name for the devil, who is also called Satan.
6:16: τίς δὲ συνκατάθεσις ναῷ Θεοῦ μετὰ εἰδώλων
Here, just as in 6:14–15, Paul is using the question form to deny that something could be true.
Here Paul speaks as if we were a temple. He follows this metaphor with a quotation which illustrates how God dwells with his people as their God.

Here, the phrase the living God identifies God as the one who lives and possibly as the one who gives life. The primary point is that God is actually alive, unlike idols and other things that people call their gods.
These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
Here the author of the quotation speaks as if God would walk among his people. He means that God will be as close to his people as if he were walking around with them.
Here the word translated as themselves switches focus from God to they.
6:17: ἐξέλθατε ἐκ μέσου αὐτῶν καὶ ἀφορίσθητε
Here, these two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
Here the author of the quotation uses the word touch to refer to interacting with someone in any way, not just by touching it.
6:18: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
7:1: Here Paul is referring to the promises from the Old Testament that he quoted in 6:16–18, which indicate that believers are God’s people, that God will welcome them, and that they are God’s sons and daughters.

Here Paul uses the word flesh to refer to the outward part of people, particularly the body. He uses the word spirit to refer to the inward part of people, the part that thinks, feels, and makes decisions.
The word perfecting could introduce: (1) another thing that believers should do while they are cleansing themselves; (2) the result of the “cleansing.”; (3) how they “cleanse” themselves.
7:2: Here, just as in 6:11–13, Paul speaks of loving others as if it were about having space for others in one’s insides. When people have space for other people inside them, they are loving and caring for them.
οὐδένα ἠδικήσαμεν, οὐδένα ἐφθείραμεν, οὐδένα ἐπλεονεκτήσαμεν

Here Paul uses three phrases with similar structure and meaning to strongly deny that he did anything to hurt any of the Corinthians. It is possible that the word wronged refers to doing something unjust, the word ruined refers to corrupting or perverting someone, and the phrase took advantage of refers to gaining money or things from somebody without doing anything in return.
7:3: Here Paul refers to what he said in the previous verse about how he and his fellow workers did not hurt anyone (7:2). Here he wishes to clarify that he does not mean that it was the Corinthians who hurt people.
Here Paul speaks as if the Corinthians were in the hearts of him and his fellow workers. He means that they love the Corinthians very much.
Here Paul refers to two extreme alternates, dying and living, to indicate that nothing that happens will keep him and his fellow workers from loving the Corinthians.
7:4: Here Paul could be saying that he: (1) is confident that they follow Christ and do what is right; (2) can speak boldly or confidently to them.
Here Paul speaks as if he were “overflowing” with joy. He means that he has so much joy that he feels like it has completely filled him up.
7:5: Here, the phrase our flesh refers to the whole person. Paul uses it to emphasize the physical or bodily nature of their suffering.
Here Paul continues what he was saying in 2:13 about how he “had no relief” in his “spirit.” What he means is that traveling to Macedonia did not help with his concerns about Titus or his sufferings.
Here, the word without identifies the source of the conflicts as external to Paul and those with him. The word within identifies the source of the fears as internal to Paul and his fellow workers.
7:7: Here, the phrase for my sake modifies all three items in this list. The Corinthians experience longing to see Paul, they experience mourning because they grieved Paul, and they have zeal for Paul.
Here, Paul speaks about how his joy upon receiving the report from Titus is even more than the joy that he already described in 7:4.
7:8: Here Paul again refers to a letter that he previously sent to them.
Here, the word seeing refers generally to “knowing” something, not just to looking with one’s eyes.
Here Paul uses the word hour to refer to a short period of time, but he does not specify how short.
7:9: The implication is that the phrase with respect to God indicates that how the Corinthians were grieved was how God desires people to be grieved.
Here the word translated as so that could introduce: (1) a result; (2) a purpose.
Here Paul explains that the Corinthians were not harmed or injured in any way by how they were grieved.
7:10: Here Paul uses words very similar to those he used in 7:9: “you were grieved with respect to God.” Use a similar form to what you used there.

Here, the phrase without regret could describe: (1) how those who have sorrow with respect to God do not experience regret; (2) how Paul does not have regret for how he caused the Corinthians to feel sorrow.
Here, the word world refers to the people in the world who do not believe in Jesus.
Here, the word death refers not only to physical death but also to spiritual death.
7:11: Here, the phrase to be made sorrowful with respect to God further defines what this same thing is.
Here, just as in 7:9–10, the phrase with respect to God indicates that how the Corinthians were sorrowful was how God desires people to be sorrowful.
Here, the phrase this matter refers to what happened at Corinth that caused Paul to write the previous letter. Paul has already discussed this incident in 2:3–11, so he simply refers to it here.
7:12: Here, the phrase I wrote refers to the previous letter that Paul sent to the Corinthians.

Here, Paul refers to something being revealed before God to indicate a close connection to God. The phrase could indicate that: (1) God testifies to or approves the Corinthians’ earnestness; (2) the Corinthians recognize their earnestness when they are in God’s presence.
7:13: ἀναπέπαυται τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ πάντων ὑμῶν
Here Paul speaks as if Titus’ spirit were a tired body that needed to be refreshed. He could mean that Titus: (1) was encouraged or given new energy; (2) was no longer worried about the Corinthians.
7:14: Here Paul could be referring to: (1) everything he has told the Corinthians, including the gospel; (2) specifically what he told the Corinthians about his travel plans.
7:15: Here, the phrase more abundant could indicate that: (1) Titus has more affections for them than he did before he visited them; (2) Titus simply has a great deal of affections.
Here, the Corinthians’ obedience could be directed toward: (1) Paul and his fellow workers, including Titus; (2) just Titus.
Here the Corinthians’ fear could be directed toward: (1) Titus as Paul’s representative; (2) the consequences of what had happened; (3) God, whom Titus represented.
The terms fear and trembling mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.
7:16: The implication is that Paul is confident that the Corinthians are doing what is right or proper.
8:1: Paul is using the term brothers to mean people who share the same faith.
As Paul indicates in 7:5, he is in Macedonia when he writes this letter.
8:2: Here Paul is speaking of poverty as if it were a deep hole. He means that they were very poor.
Here Paul is speaking of generosity as if it were riches. He means that these people had very much generosity, just like a rich person has very much money.
8:3: Here, the phrase of their own accord indicates that no one forced or required the believers in Macedonia to act as they did. Rather, they chose to do so on their own.
8:4: The two words favor and fellowship work together to express a single idea. The word fellowship describes what the favor is.
τῆς διακονίας τῆς εἰς τοὺς ἁγίους

Here Paul does not give very many details about the ministry because he had already told the Corinthians about it in 1 Corinthians 16:1–4. From that passage and other passages, we know that Paul was collecting money from various churches to send to Jerusalem to help the believers there.
8:5: Here Paul is implying that the Macedonians did more than Paul and his fellow workers had hoped, not that they did less.
Here Paul speaks as if the Macedonians were gifts that they themselves gave to the Lord and to us. He means that the Macedonians chose to completely serve and honor the Lord and us.
Here, the words first and then could indicate what is: (1) more and less important; (2) first and second in sequence.

Here, the phrase and then could introduce: (1) what comes after what they first did; (2) the second part of what they first did. Paul implies that what comes after what they first did is giving money.
8:6: Here Paul could be implying that Titus already began: (1) the grace, which is collecting money for the believers in Jerusalem; (2) to work for the sake of the Corinthians in general.
Here, the word grace refers to what it did in 8:4: being able to contribute money to what Paul was collecting for believers in Jerusalem. If possible, translate it as you did in 8:4.
8:7: Paul says everything here as a generalization for emphasis.
Many ancient manuscripts read from us in you.

Here, the phrase from us in you could indicate that: (1) the love is how Paul and his fellow workers feel about the Corinthians; (2) Paul and those with him enabled or caused the Corinthians to have love.
Here, the word grace refers to what it did in 8:4, 6: being able to contribute money to what Paul was collecting for believers in Jerusalem. If possible, translate it as you did in those verses.
8:8: Here, the phrase through the earnestness of others indicates the standard by which Paul is proving the love of the Corinthians.
8:9: Here, Paul is speaking of what God considers valuable, including blessings, power, and honor, as if it were wealth.
8:10: In these phrases, Paul is speaking about collecting money for the believers in Jerusalem.
8:11: He does not want them to borrow money or give everything that they own.
8:12: Here Paul does not state what is fully acceptable. He implies that it is whatever they give that is fully acceptable.
8:13: Here, the phrase out of equality could provide: (1) the basis or principle for giving and sharing; (2) the desired result from giving and sharing.
8:14: Here, the phrase At the present time could refer to: (1) how things were when Paul wrote this letter. In this case, Paul is telling the Corinthians that they have more than the Jerusalem believers do, and so they should help. In the future, if the Jerusalem believers have more than the Corinthians, they will help the Corinthians; (2) the time between Christ’s first and second comings. In this case, Paul is telling the Corinthians that they should help the Jerusalem believers financially, and the Jerusalem believers will help them spiritually.
8:15: Here Paul is quoting from a story about how God led the Israelites through the desert. They did not have much food, so God miraculously made something like bread appear on the ground for them. The Israelites called the food “manna,” and God commanded each of them to gather a specific amount for each person. This amount was just right, which is what this quotation describes.

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.

9:8: Here, the word grace refers primarily to good things that God has given to the Corinthians, including money and possessions.

Here, the phrase endures to eternity could mean that: (1) the person always does what is righteous; (2) God will always remember and reward the righteous things that the person does.
9:10: Here Paul applies what he said about actual seed and bread in the first half of the verse to what he is telling the Corinthians about giving to fellow believers. He means that God will give them the means to give (the seed) and will enable their gifts to really help others (increasing the fruit).
9:11: Here, the phrase being enriched does indicate that the Corinthians have more than enough money and possessions. Paul’s point is that God gives them more than they need so that they can share it with others.

Here, the phrase through us shows that Paul and his fellow workers are involved in how the generosity leads to thanksgiving. More specifically, they are the ones who collect and send the gifts to fellow believers.
9:12: Here, the phrase this service refers specifically to collecting and sending money to help the believers in Jerusalem.

Here, the phrase to the gospel of Christ could go with: (1) obedience. In this case, they are obedient to the gospel of Christ; (2) confession. In this case, they confess to the gospel of Christ.

10:1: Here Paul describes himself with words that the Corinthians or his enemies use. He does not mean that he thinks these words are actually true about himself, but he repeats them to respond to what others are saying.
Here, the phrase face to face refers to being with someone physically or in person.
The terms meekness and gentleness mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.
10:2: Here Paul implies that he will be courageous as he argues against or defends himself against the people who are saying bad things about him.

Here Paul refers to people who are often called “the opponents.” It is not clear whether these people are some of the Corinthians or whether they have visited the Corinthians. What is clear is that they are saying bad things about Paul and claiming to have greater authority and a better gospel.
Paul uses the term walking to speak of behavior in life.
Here Paul uses the phrase according to the flesh to refer to human ways of thinking and acting.

If possible, express this idea so that it is clearly connected to how you translate according to the flesh.

Paul does not mean that they are actually killing people or fighting with physical weapons. If possible, preserve the metaphor or express the idea with a simile.

He defines the strongholds as strategies or arguments against him and the gospel. Paul means by this that God empowers him and his fellow workers to prove that these arguments are false. Paul does not mean that they are physically fighting against people or destroying physical strongholds.
Here, fleshly represents what is natural and human as opposed to what is spiritual and godly.
Here, the phrase powerful to God indicates that the weapons are powerful because God makes them powerful.
The phrases the tearing down of strongholds and tearing down strategies mean similar things. Paul is using the two phrases together for emphasis, with the second phrase defining the first phrase.
10:5: Here, just as in 10:3–4, Paul speaks as if he and his fellow workers were involved in a war. In this verse, he speaks about every high thing, which are fortifications or walls. Just as the victor in a war takes the conquered people captive, so Paul and his fellow workers wish to take peoples’ thoughts captive so that these people are obedient to Christ. If possible, preserve the metaphor or express the idea with a simile.
Here, the phrase every thought could refer to: (1) the thoughts had by people who oppose the gospel; (2) the thoughts had by believers.
10:6: Here Paul finishes speaking as if he and his fellow workers were involved in a war. Here he says that they are in readiness, like soldiers ready to attack. When they attack, they will avenge every act of disobedience. What he means is that, once people are captive to the “obedience of Christ,” he and his fellow workers will punish them if they go back to being disobedient. If possible, preserve the metaphor or express the idea with a simile.
Here, the word obedience could refer to being obedient: (1) to Christ. This option is supported by the phrase “the obedience of Christ” in 10:5; (2) to Paul.

Here Paul is referring to how he wants the Corinthians to commit to obeying. When they always work towards obedience, then he and his fellow workers will avenge every act of disobedience. He does not mean that the Corinthians need to be perfectly obedient or complete specific acts of obedience.
10:7: This sentence could be: (1) a command to look at what is obvious; (2) a rebuke concerning how they only look at how things appear.
Here Paul uses a third-person imperative.
10:8: Here, the phrase somewhat excessively could mean that Paul is boasting: (1) more than some people would consider proper; (2) a great deal; (3) more than he already has.
εἰς οἰκοδομὴν καὶ οὐκ εἰς καθαίρεσιν ὑμῶν
Here, Paul is speaking of the Corinthian believers as if they were a building.
10:9: Here Paul refers in general to letters he sends to the Corinthians. He is probably including both 1 Corinthians and the other “severe” letter he has already mentioned.
10:10: Here, Paul is speaking of letters as if they were objects that were weighty. He could mean that people think the letters are: (1) severe or burdensome; (2) important or impressive.
The terms weighty and forceful mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.
Here, the phrase bodily presence refers to how a person looks and acts when they are around other people.
10:11: Here Paul uses a third-person imperative.
Here, the word word represents what someone says in words.

Here Paul could be comparing what he and his fellow workers are like in our word with what they: (1) are like in our deed. Here, the word deed refers to what Paul and his fellow workers do and will do.

Here Paul does not state what it is that these people do not understand. What he means is that these people are not acting in wise ways.

Here Paul speaks as if a measure could reach out and touch a person. He means that the measure includes the Corinthians in what it measures.
Here, the phrase that reached even as far as you indicates that the measure includes the Corinthians as something that Paul and his fellow workers can boast about.
10:14: Here Paul is indicating that he and his fellow workers have not gone beyond the “limit” that he refers to in 10:13.
Here Paul refers to what would need to be true if he and his fellow workers were actually overextending themselves. That would be true only if they did not reach or visit the Corinthians.

Here, the phrase we came could indicate that: (1) Paul and his fellow workers had already visited the Corinthians; (2) Paul and his fellow workers visited the Corinthians before Paul’s opponents visited the Corinthians.
10:15: Here Paul does not state directly what is enlarged. He could mean that: (1) their ministry or work might be enlarged; (2) they might be enlarged or praised by the Corinthians.

11:1: Here, the foolishness that Paul refers to is how he is about to boast about his qualifications as an apostle. Paul considers this to be foolishness, but he will boast anyways to help the Corinthians realize that he and the gospel that he preaches come from God.
Here, this clause could be: (1) a statement of what the Corinthians are already doing, either as they listen to this letter or in the past when Paul visited them; (2) a command to act in this way.
11:2: Here, the phrase godly jealousy could refer to jealousy: (1) that is the same jealousy that God has; (2) that is from God.
Here Paul speaks as if he is the father of the Corinthians, who together are his daughter. Paul has promised to give his daughter (the Corinthians) as a wife to a man, who is Christ.

11:4: Here Paul could be referring to: (1) any person or group of people; (2) a specific person whom Paul knows about.

11:6: Here Paul is referring to the practice of speaking in public in order to persuade many people.
Here, the word knowledge refers to what a person knows about Jesus and the good news about him.

Here Paul could be referring to: (1) what he has already said and what he is about to say; (2) what Paul is about to say in the following verses; (3) what Paul has already said.

Here, the phrase his hands represents the power or servants of the “ethnarch,” that is, the local ruler of the city.
