Here Paul refers to a common question related to stories about people traveling to heaven: in what way does the person ascend into heaven? There were three primary ways a person could ascend: they could go into heaven physically in their body, they could go into heaven in a dream, or they could go into heaven with only their non-physical part, that is, their spirit. Here Paul indicates that he does not know in what way the man in Christ ascended into heaven.
Here Paul repeats I do not know in order to emphasize his lack of knowledge.

Many people in Paul’s culture believed that the space that they called “heaven” contained multiple layers or spheres of individual heavens. Here, Paul refers to the third heaven. Since he does not specify how many heavens he thinks there are, it is best not to clarify whether this is the highest heaven or not.
12:3: Here Paul again addresses the question about whether the man went into heaven in bodily form or not. He uses almost the same words he used in 12:2, although he does not repeat I do not know here.
12:4: Here, the word Paradise refers to a place in heaven where those who have trusted in God live after they die and before Jesus comes back.
ἄρρητα ῥήματα, ἃ οὐκ ἐξὸν ἀνθρώπῳ λαλῆσαι

The terms inexpressible and which are not permitted for a man to speak mean similar things. It is possible that inexpressible indicates that people are unable to speak these amazing words, and which are not permitted indicates that God does not allow people to speak these words.
12:6: Here, the phrase think more of me refers to how people can think a person is greater or more powerful than they actually are.
ὃ βλέπει με, ἢ ἀκούει ἐξ ἐμοῦ
Here Paul refers to what people can observe him doing and saying. He wants people to think about him only based on what they see him doing and hear him saying.
12:7: Here Paul speaks as if a thorn was stabbing him in the flesh. He could mean that: (1) he had a sickness or ailment that affected his flesh, that is, his body; (2) people opposed him and his ministry; (3) a demon attacked him.
Here Paul refers to a messenger or angel that came from or was sent by Satan, the devil.
Here Paul speaks as if the messenger of Satan were physically buffeting or hitting him. He means that the messenger caused him to suffer in some physical way.

Here most ancient manuscripts include the clause so that I would not become super arrogant. Some ancient manuscripts do not have this clause. Most likely, this clause was accidentally omitted because Paul had already said it once.
12:8: Here, the subject of remove could be: (1) the Lord, who can remove the thorn and the suffering it causes; (2) the thorn, or messenger of Satan, which can remove itself from Paul.
12:9: Here, the phrase even more could indicate that Paul will: (1) boast more in his weaknesses than he has already; (2) boast in his weaknesses rather than praying for the removal of the thorn; (3) boast in his weaknesses rather than in his strengths.

Here Paul speaks as if the power of Christ were a person who could reside in or upon Paul, who is pictured like a tent or house. He means that the power of Christ consistently becomes part of his life and is something that he can always have.
12:10: Here Paul means that he is content with these bad experiences and is even happy that he experiences them, because Christ works through him when these bad things happen. He does not mean that he enjoys the bad experiences themselves.
12:11: Here Paul means that he has spoken in foolish ways in the previous several chapters. He does not mean that he is always a foolish person.
Here Paul means is that reason why he had to speak in foolish ways is that the Corinthians were behaving wrongly.
Here, the word translated as yourselves emphasizes you.
Here Paul could be using the past tense because: (1) he is referring to the time when he was with the Corinthians; (2) he is speaking of what is generally true.

Here Paul refers to his opponents, the false teachers, with the words that they themselves or their followers used to describe them: “super-apostles”. He does not actually believe that these people are better apostles or greater than anyone else.
Here Paul speaks as if he were actually nothing. What he means is that he himself is not great or powerful at all without Christ working through him.
12:12: ὑπομονῇ— σημείοις τε, καὶ τέρασιν, καὶ δυνάμεσιν
Here, the list, both signs and wonders and miracles, could be: (1) examples of what the signs of an apostle were; (2) the ways in which Paul demonstrated the signs of an apostle.
σημείοις τε, καὶ τέρασιν, καὶ δυνάμεσιν

Here Paul uses three similar words to describe supernatural acts that God empowered Paul to do. The word signs emphasizes that these acts reveal something; the word wonders emphasizes that these acts are amazing or unusual; the word miracles emphasizes that these acts are powerful. Paul uses these three words to show that he performed various acts that showed that he was an apostle.
12:13: Here Paul speaks from the perspective of his opponents, who tell the Corinthians that Paul has committed an injustice in treating them worse than the other churches by not asking them for money. He speaks from their perspective to show the Corinthians that this perspective is foolish and wrong.
Paul is using the question form to show the Corinthians that he treated them like all the other churches except for not asking for money.
Here Paul refers to the other churches that he works with.
Here Paul speaks of asking for money as if it were a heavy burden that he would have asked the Corinthians to carry for him.
Here, the word translated as myself emphasizes I.
12:14: Here Paul speaks of asking for money as if it were a heavy burden that he could have asked the Corinthians to carry for him.

Here Paul contrasts the things that the Corinthians have, or their possessions, with the Corinthians themselves. What he means is that he does not want the money and possessions that the Corinthians have. Instead, he wants the Corinthians themselves; that is, he wants them to trust him and Jesus.

Here Paul speaks of himself as a parent and the Corinthians as his children. In Paul’s culture, parents generally saved money for their children to use. Paul uses this custom to illustrate how he, as a parent, should be giving to the Corinthians instead of the Corinthians, as children, giving to him.
12:15: Here Paul speaks as if his energy, time, and even he himself were money that he or someone else could spend. He means that he is willing to use all his energy and time and even to experience hardships and difficulties to help the Corinthians.
Here, the phrase your souls represents the Corinthians.
εἰ περισσοτέρως ὑμᾶς ἀγαπῶν, ἧσσον ἀγαπῶμαι
Paul is using the question form to rebuke the Corinthians for loving him less when he loves them more abundantly.

Here Paul uses two comparison words without indicating exactly what he is comparing. He could mean that: (1) his love is increasing in comparison to the Corinthians’ love, which is decreasing; (2) he has much love, while the Corinthians have little love; (3) his love for them is greater than his love for other churches, while the Corinthians love him less than other churches do.
12:16: ἔστω δέ, ἐγὼ οὐ κατεβάρησα ὑμᾶς; ἀλλὰ

Here, the phrase But let it be {so} indicates that something is agreed upon or certainly true. Paul could be referring to: (1) what he is about to say about not being a burden to the Corinthians. He means that he and the Corinthians can agree about that; (2) what he said in the previous verse about loving the Corinthians, although he may be loved less. He means that even if that is true, he will still not burden the Corinthians.
Here, the word translated as myself emphasizes I.
Here Paul speaks of asking for money as if it were a heavy burden that he would have asked the Corinthians to carry for him.
ἀλλὰ ὑπάρχων πανοῦργος δόλῳ, ὑμᾶς ἔλαβον

Here Paul speaks from the perspective of either the Corinthians of the opponents. They may think or say that Paul was crafty and caught them by deceit. He speaks from their perspective so that he can respond to this claim in the following verses.
Here Paul speaks of deceiving or tricking the Corinthians as if he were physically grabbing them. See the similar phrase “takes advantage” in 11:20.
12:17: Paul is using the question form to deny that any person he has sent to the Corinthians has cheated them.
12:18: παρεκάλεσα Τίτον καὶ συναπέστειλα τὸν ἀδελφόν
Here Paul refers to a trip Titus took previously to visit the Corinthians. He is probably referring to the visit he mentions in 8:6.
Paul is using the term brother to mean a person who shares the same faith.
Paul is using the question form to remind the Corinthians that Titus did not take advantage of them.
Paul is using the question form to remind the Corinthians that Titus behaved in the same ways that Paul did.
Here, the word we refers to Titus and Paul only.
Paul speaks of behavior in life as if it were walking.
Here, the word spirit could refer to: (1) the spirit of a person, which refers to the inner life of a person, that is, how that person thinks, feels, and makes decisions; (2) the Holy Spirit.

Here Paul speaks as if he and Titus walked on the same path so closely together that the person walking behind stepped in the footsteps of the person in front. He means that they did and said very similar things.
12:19: Paul is using the question form to deny that what he has said is primarily for the purpose of defending ourselves.
Here, the phrase all of this time refers to everything that Paul has written so far in this letter.

Here, just as with the phrase “in the presence of God” in 2:17, the phrase Before God could indicate that: (1) Paul and his fellow workers speak as they do because they know that God sees or knows what they do. So, they speak in a way that pleases God; (2) Paul and his fellow workers speak with God as a witness guaranteeing what they say.

Here Paul uses the spatial metaphor in Christ to describe the union of believers with Christ. In this case, being in Christ, or united to Christ, explains that Paul and his fellow workers speak from their perspective as those united to Christ.
Here, the phrase all these things refers primarily to what Paul has written in this letter so far. However, it also includes everything that Paul and his fellow workers say and do.
Here, Paul is speaking of the Corinthian believers as if they were a building.
12:20: οὐχ οἵους θέλω … οἷον οὐ θέλετε
Here Paul refers to how both he and the Corinthians have ideas about how they think the other person should be behaving. He fears that these ideas will not be accurate.
Here Paul implies that they are doing all these wrong things within their own group. He does not mean that they are doing these things to people outside their group.
12:21: ταπεινώσῃ με ὁ Θεός μου πρὸς ὑμᾶς, καὶ

Here Paul could be implying that God will humble him: (1) because he would feel ashamed about how the Corinthians were acting; (2) because he would have to use his authority for tearing down instead of building up; (3) because he would mourn publicly.
τῇ ἀκαθαρσίᾳ, καὶ πορνείᾳ, καὶ ἀσελγείᾳ
The terms impurity, sexual immorality, and debauchery mean similar things. Paul is using the three terms together to include all types of sexual sin.
13:1: Paul is quoting here from Deuteronomy 19:15. He has been accusing the Corinthian believers of doing wrong, and so he compares the number of his visits, during which he has observed and will observe this wrong behavior, with the number of witnesses that the Old Testament required for convicting someone of doing wrong.
Paul is using the term mouth to mean the words that people say by using their mouths.
13:2: The implication is that, when Paul comes, he will punish any believer there who is continuing to live sinfully.
13:3: The implication is that Christ will be powerful among the Corinthian believers when Paul comes and disciplines them using Christ’s power.
13:4: Here, Paul is speaking of his relationship to Christ as if he were inside of Christ.
13:5: These two phrases mean the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
The word translated as yourselves is plural, referring to all of the Corinthian believers. However, the meaning is that each believer is to examine himself, not that they should examine each other.
Here, Paul is speaking of faith as if it were something which the Corinthians could be inside.
Paul is using the question form here to emphasize to the Corinthian believers something that is true: that Jesus Christ does live in them.

Here, in you could mean: (1) Jesus is intimately connected to each believing individual, as if Jesus were living inside each person; (2) Jesus is living among them, part of and the most important member of the group.
13:6: Here the word ourselves emphasizes that Paul is talking about his apostolic team, who introduced the Corinthian believers to Jesus Christ.
Paul is referring here to himself and his apostolic team, who introduced the Corinthian believers to Jesus Christ.
13:7: Paul uses the words ourselves and yourselves to emphasize the difference between his thinking and the thinking of the Corinthian believers. He wants only good for them, while they suspect that he wants only good for himself.
13:9: Here, as in verse 7, the words ourselves and yourselves emphasize the difference between Paul and the Corinthian believers. He wants them to be strong in the Lord, and it does not matter if people think that he is weak.
13:10: εἰς οἰκοδομὴν καὶ οὐκ εἰς καθαίρεσιν
Here, Paul is speaking of the Corinthian believers as if they were a building.
13:11: Here, think the same means to agree on the most important things and to not argue about the lesser things.
13:12: A holy kiss was a symbolic action to show familial love between believers. In some cultures, a kiss as a greeting is appropriate, but in other cultures it is not appropriate. The idea of a holy kiss is that it be a greeting that is appropriate in the culture, whether it be a kiss, a hug, a handshake, or something else, and also that it be holy, that is, appropriate between God’s people.
These saints are the fellow believers who are there with Paul.
13:13: Paul ends his letter with this blessing.
